UNIT 6: VOLCANIC ACTIVITY AND IMPACTS

KEY THEME
- Volcanoes are created by powerful forces within the Earth.
- Volcanic activity has created some of the Earth's most interesting landforms and has a big impact on people who live nearby.
- Learning outcomes: describe volcanic activity at constructive (divergent) and destructive (convergent) plate boundaries and at hotspots; explain the processes and the landforms they make, using Irish and international examples; investigate the economic, environmental and social impacts of volcanic activity in one Global North setting (Iceland) and one Global South setting (the Philippines).

KEY TERMS
- Basic lava: a runny, non-explosive lava.
- Acidic lava: a thick, explosive lava.
- Shield volcano: a gently sloping volcanic cone.
- Stratovolcano: a steep-sided volcanic cone (also called a composite volcano).
- Fissure: a crack or opening in the Earth's crust.
- Viscosity: describes how the lava flows. High viscosity = thick and sticky, flows slowly, like honey. Low viscosity = runny, spreads easily and flows fast, like warm syrup.
- Lava plateau: a large, flat area formed by many layers of lava flowing out of cracks in the Earth during repeated volcanic eruptions.
- Lahar: a fast-moving volcanic mudflow made of water, ash and rocks that travels down the slopes of a volcano like wet concrete. Lahars can be triggered by eruptions or heavy rain.
- Batholith: a huge mass of magma that rises into the crust but does not reach the surface; it cools slowly underground to form coarse-grained granite.
- Subduction: when a heavier (denser) oceanic plate is forced beneath another plate at a convergent boundary.
- Hotspot: an unusually hot region in the Earth's mantle (a mantle plume) that makes superheated magma which rises through the crust to form volcanoes.

LIFE CYCLE OF A VOLCANO
- Active: currently erupting, has erupted recently or shows signs it could erupt again. Examples: Kilauea (Hawaii, US), Mt Etna (Italy), Mt St Helens (Washington, US).
- Dormant: not erupting now but could erupt again in the future. 'Sleeping' volcanoes that still have a magma supply. Examples: Mt Fuji (Japan), Mt Kilimanjaro (Tanzania), Mt Teide (Spain).
- Extinct: has not erupted for tens of thousands or millions of years and is not expected to erupt again. The magma supply is cut off. Examples: Ben Nevis (UK), Slemish (Co. Antrim, Northern Ireland).

STRUCTURE OF A VOLCANO (Figure 6.2 in words)
- Magma chamber: holds the molten material below the surface.
- Central vent: connected to the magma chamber; the main passageway for magma to travel to the surface.
- Side (secondary) vent: a smaller passage branching off the main vent.
- Crater: the mouth of the volcano, where ash, lava, hot rocks and gases escape.
- Lava: the name for molten material once it reaches the Earth's surface (below the surface it is magma).
- Cone: the cone-shaped hill formed over time as layers of ash, lava and volcanic material build up. Old layers of ash and lava make up the cone.
- Above the crater: a cloud of steam, gas and ash.

MATERIAL EMITTED DURING AN ERUPTION
- Lava (basic or acidic - see table below).
- Ash: a grey or black powder of tiny pieces of rock and glass. Wind can carry it over large distances, covering the whole landscape.
- Volcanic bombs: large pieces of rock thrown out of the volcano with force.
- Volcanic gases: steam (water vapour), sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and chlorine. These can be highly toxic, causing breathing problems and acid rain.
- Pyroclastic flows: clouds of hot gas, ash and rock that move at speed down the side of a volcano, destroying everything in their path.
- Lahars: mudflows of water, ash and debris.

BASIC LAVA vs ACIDIC LAVA
- Silica content: basic is low (about 50%); acidic is high (about 70%).
- Viscosity: basic is low (fluid, runny); acidic is high (thick, sticky).
- Flow: basic flows quickly and covers large distances; acidic flows slowly and does not travel far.
- Gas: in basic lava gases escape easily; in acidic lava gases are trapped, so pressure builds up.
- Eruption style: basic = gentle, less explosive; acidic = violent, explosive.
- Volcano shape: basic = broad, gently sloping shield volcanoes; acidic = steep-sided composite/stratovolcanoes.
- Typical location: basic = divergent boundaries (e.g. mid-ocean ridges) and hotspots; acidic = convergent boundaries (subduction zones).
- Examples: basic = Mauna Loa (Hawaii, US); acidic = Mt St Helens (US), Mt Etna (Italy), Mt Pinatubo (Philippines).

WHERE VOLCANIC ACTIVITY OCCURS (Figure 6.4)
- Mainly along convergent and divergent plate boundaries and at hotspots.
- Five key locations shown: 1. island arc (subduction zone); 2. hotspot; 3. mid-ocean ridge (sea-floor spreading); 4. volcanic arc (subduction zone); 5. rifting (on continental crust). Convection currents in the mantle drive the plate movement.

VOLCANIC ACTIVITY AT CONVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Caused by subduction: when an oceanic plate collides with another plate (oceanic or continental), the heavier oceanic plate is forced beneath the other.
- The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the less dense continental plate.
- The subducting plate sinks into the mantle. Heat and pressure make minerals in the plate break down and release water into the mantle.
- The water lowers the melting point of the mantle, so it partially melts and creates magma.
- This magma is less dense than the surrounding rock, so it rises through the crust and causes an eruption at the surface.
- Eruptions are usually very explosive because of acidic lava (high silica and gas content).
- They form tall, steep-sided cones called stratovolcanoes. Example: Kanlaon in the Philippines.
- Stratovolcano diagram (Fig 6.5): crater, alternating layers of lava and ash, steep slope, vent, secondary vent, magma chamber; Kanlaon is 2,500 m+ high and 30 km wide.
- Key feature - volcanic arcs: chains of volcanoes in a line parallel to the subduction zone, sitting on the overriding plate.
  - Continental volcanic arcs, e.g. the Andes - an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate.
  - Volcanic island arcs, e.g. the Philippines and Japan - two oceanic plates collide.
- Key feature - earthquakes: as plates collide, stress builds and is released as an earthquake. Earthquakes at subduction zones are often frequent and powerful.
- Pacific Ring of Fire: a horseshoe-shaped zone around the edges of the Pacific Ocean with many earthquakes and eruptions. It holds about 75% of the world's active volcanoes. Caused by plate movements, especially subduction.

VOLCANIC ACTIVITY AT DIVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates slowly move away from each other, like a giant tear in the crust.
- The crust stretches and thins, so long cracks called fissures open.
- Pressure decreases in the mantle and hot magma rises through the cracks to fill the gaps.
- Very visible in Iceland, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge cuts across the island.
- The magma is basic (low in silica, runny). Lava spreads in thin, wide layers and cools quickly, forming new crust.
- Typical landforms: shield volcanoes and sometimes new islands.
- Gases escape easily, so eruptions are usually not explosive - they create new land rather than causing much destruction. These eruptions built up most of the planet's seafloor. In Iceland you can walk between two plates.
- Key feature - mid-ocean ridges: the most extensive divergent boundaries, underwater mountain ranges like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. They account for over 70% of global volcanic activity.
- Key feature - rift valleys: on land, divergent boundaries create rift valleys, e.g. the East African Rift Valley. Volcanoes form there when magma rises through fissures, e.g. Mt Kilimanjaro.
- Geofact: Iceland sits on a hotspot AND on a divergent boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, making it one of the most active volcanic regions on Earth.

VOLCANIC ACTIVITY AT HOTSPOTS
- A hotspot is an unusually hot region in the mantle, called a mantle plume. It makes superheated magma that rises through the crust to form volcanoes.
- Unlike most volcanoes, hotspot volcanoes are often in the middle of plates.
- The mantle plume is stationary (fixed). As the plate moves over it, magma breaks through the crust to form a volcano.
- The plate carries the volcano away like a conveyor belt. Cut off from its magma, it becomes extinct, and a new active volcano forms over the hotspot.
- Result: a line (chain) of volcanic islands - youngest directly over the hotspot, older extinct ones further away.
- Hawaii: Kilauea and Mauna Loa are active and sit above the hotspot. Older islands like Maui and Kauai show the path of extinct volcanoes as the Pacific Plate moves. Order from oldest to youngest (NW to SE): Kauai, Oahu, Maui, Hawaii.
- Hotspot volcanoes are typically shield volcanoes, with broad gentle slopes because of fluid basic lava.
- Mauna Loa diagram (Fig 6.13): gently sloping sides, layers of solidified lava, crater, vent, magma chamber; over 4,100 m above sea level (5,000 m+ more below), about 180 km wide. Compare Kanlaon: 2,500 m+ high, 30 km wide, steep.

VOLCANIC LANDFORMS (formed when lava flows on the surface and solidifies)
- Shield volcano: basic lava erupts from a central vent or fissures; runny lava spreads in thin, wide layers, building a broad, gently sloping mountain. Repeated eruptions add layers. Eruptions gentle. Examples: Mauna Loa, Kilauea (Hawaii, US).
- Stratovolcano (composite volcano): layers of thick, sticky acidic lava and volcanic ash build up after many eruptions. Lava does not flow far, so it gathers near the vent, making a steep-sided cone. Eruptions often explosive (gas-rich, high-silica magma). Examples: Mt St Helens (US), Mt Fuji (Japan).
- Cinder cone: forms after an explosive eruption when gas-rich lava blasts into the air and breaks into tiny pieces called cinders (hot, rocky fragments). They fall back around the vent and pile up into a steep, cone-shaped hill with a wide bowl-like crater. Usually small; can form quickly, often after one eruption. Example: Paricutin (Mexico).
- Lava dome: very thick, sticky lava moves slowly up the vent; too thick to flow far, so it piles up around the vent as a small, rounded, steep-sided mound. Grows as more lava squeezes up. Examples: Mt St Helens lava dome (US), Puy de Dome (France).
- Caldera: a stratovolcano erupts so much magma in a huge explosive eruption that the magma chamber is left almost empty. With no support, the top collapses inwards, making a massive bowl-shaped depression, which may fill with rainwater to form a lake. Three stages: magma chamber full; eruption empties it; collapse forms caldera (with ash and a resurgent dome). Examples: Yellowstone caldera (Wyoming, US), Crater Lake (Oregon, US).
- Geyser: a hot water spring. Water seeps into underground chambers and is heated by hot rocks or magma. Trapped in narrow passages, it becomes superheated and pressure builds. When pressure is too great a powerful jet of hot water and steam explodes out. The chamber refills and the cycle repeats. Examples: Old Faithful (Yellowstone, US), Strokkur (Iceland).
- Fissure volcano / lava plateau: low-viscosity basic lava erupts from long cracks instead of a central vent, spreading over large areas and solidifying into thick, layered plateaus. Examples: Grindavik fissure eruptions (Iceland), Antrim Plateau (Northern Ireland).

IRISH CASE STUDY 1: THE ANTRIM PLATEAU
- Formed about 65 million years ago by intense volcanic activity linked to the separation of the Eurasian and American plates (divergent boundary).
- Fissure eruptions: highly fluid basic lava rose through cracks and spread over the landscape, cooling into a wide, flat basalt plateau.
- Eruptions were non-violent (lava low in gas), so lava spread over long distances. This went on and off for about 2 million years.
- Layer upon layer of basalt built up, up to 1 km thick in places.
- As the lava cooled it contracted and fractured, forming hexagonal columns - the Giant's Causeway (over 40,000 columns).
- Older sedimentary rocks (chalk and limestone) lie beneath the basalt, laid down when shallow seas covered the area.
- A major landmark in Northern Ireland; a UNESCO World Heritage Site and popular tourist attraction.

IRISH CASE STUDY 2: THE LEINSTER BATHOLITH
- A batholith forms when a large amount of magma is produced at colliding plate boundaries. It rises into the crust but does not reach the surface. Trapped deep down, it cools very slowly into coarse-grained granite.
- Over millions of years uplift and erosion remove the rock above and expose the batholith.
- The Leinster Batholith stretches over 120 km and forms the core of the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains (running through Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare, Carlow, Kilkenny and Wexford, to Mt Leinster).
- Formed over 400 million years ago when the Eurasian and North American plates collided.
- Heat from the granite 'baked' the surrounding shale and sandstone, turning them into schist, slate and quartzite (metamorphism) - a band of hard metamorphic rock.
- Weathering and erosion stripped away the metamorphic cap, exposing the granite.
- Today the granite forms dome-shaped mountains such as Kippure (Co. Wicklow), while resistant metamorphic peaks such as Lugnaquilla stand tall.
- Diagram: (a) before exposure - batholith under overlying rocks with a band of metamorphic rock around it; (b) after exposure - granite at surface (Kippure), metamorphic rock (Lugnaquilla).

IMPACTS OF VOLCANIC ACTIVITY - GLOBAL NORTH vs GLOBAL SOUTH
- Global North countries usually face fewer casualties and less disruption due to strong infrastructure and effective disaster response.
- Global South countries often have higher death tolls, more displacement and longer recovery because of poorer infrastructure, limited resources and weaker emergency planning.

CASE STUDY: ICELAND (GLOBAL NORTH)
- On the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the Eurasian and North American plates separate. Frequent eruptions, especially on the Reykjanes Peninsula (south-west).
Positive economic:
- Tourism: the 2010 Eyjafjallajokull eruption sparked a tourism campaign. Visitors rose from under 500,000 in 2010 to over 1.6 million in 2022, creating thousands of jobs.
- Tourism revenue graph (Fig 6.27): tourism as % of GDP rose from about 3.5% in 2009 to over 8% by 2016-2019, fell sharply to 2.8% in 2020 (lowest), then recovered to 3.9% in 2021 and 6.1% in 2022.
- Geothermal energy: clean, renewable, affordable electricity and heating. Supplies electricity to 90% of Icelandic homes, plus greenhouses, swimming pools and industries. Less need for imported fossil fuels: lower energy costs and emissions, better air quality. Energy-intensive industries like aluminium smelting get a competitive edge from cheap energy. Saves the government billions and protects the economy from rising oil prices.
- Greenhouses heated by geothermal energy allow year-round growing of vegetables, flowers and crops, supporting local producers and reducing expensive food imports.
Positive social:
- Geothermal pools and spas (e.g. the Blue Lagoon) are popular for health and wellbeing, improving quality of life.
- Low emissions and less air pollution improve public health over the long term, cutting healthcare costs.
Positive environmental:
- Geothermal energy is renewable; cleaner air, lower carbon footprint. It has reduced Iceland's CO2 emissions by up to 37%.
- Volcanic ash enriched ocean waters with minerals like iron, boosting plankton and creating richer fishing grounds in the North Atlantic.
- Over 100,000 flights in Europe were grounded after the 2010 eruption, preventing an estimated 2.8 million tonnes of CO2.
Negative economic:
- Eruptions destroy homes, roads and public buildings. Repair costs have reached US$177 million in recent years; some events cost up to 5.5% of GDP. The 2023-2024 Grindavik eruption destroyed houses and forced major rebuilding of roads and bridges.
- The 2010 Eyjafjallajokull eruption grounded flights across Europe, causing US$4.8 billion in global losses. Businesses like the Blue Lagoon faced short-term closures and job losses.
- Expensive infrastructure: lava barriers and protective dykes around the Svartsengi geothermal plant; monitoring and emergency planning add ongoing costs.
Negative social:
- Evacuations and sometimes permanent loss of community: the 1973 Heimaey eruption made 800 residents move and never return. In Grindavik 2023-2024 hundreds were displaced. Community bonds weaken.
- Ashfall poisons water supplies and reduces air quality (breathing problems). Constant threat causes fear and anxiety. Schools and healthcare disrupted.
Negative environmental:
- Air and water pollution harm health, livestock and crops. Reykjanes eruptions (2023-2025) released large amounts of sulphur dioxide (SO2); levels exceeded health limits, especially in Reykjavik, and people (especially infants and those with breathing problems) were told to stay inside.
- Lava and ash cover farmland and forestry, destroying crops, habitats and biodiversity.
- Eruptions under glaciers cause rapid ice melt and flash floods that destroy roads, bridges and farmland.
- Gas and ash clouds travel hundreds of km, causing acid rain and soil degradation.
Conclusion: the benefits from tourism and geothermal energy far outweigh the costs, making volcanic activity a net positive for Iceland.

CASE STUDY: THE PHILIPPINES (GLOBAL SOUTH)
- On the Pacific Ring of Fire with 24 active volcanoes. Activity driven by subduction of the Eurasian Plate beneath the Philippine Plate.
- Major volcanoes: Mayon, Taal, Pinatubo, Kanlaon, Bulusan (also Ragang). Frequent, sometimes highly explosive eruptions.
- Focus: Kanlaon Volcano on Negros Island, one of the most active; eruptions in 2024 and 2025.
Positive economic:
- Deep, fertile volcanic soils enriched with minerals; farmers grow rice, maize and bananas. Each eruption adds a new soil layer. Many families rely on the land; local food reduces need for expensive imports.
- Tourism draws thousands from around the world, supporting hotel staff, guides, restaurant owners, drivers and craftspeople.
- Geothermal energy from hot rocks under volcanoes like Mayon. The Philippines ranks third in the world for geothermal electricity. Less imported fuel, lower energy costs.
- Minerals: Mayon, Pinatubo and others bring gold, copper and other resources to the surface, supporting mining jobs, exports and government funds.
Positive social:
- Bigger harvests and more stable incomes let families spend more on education and healthcare, raising living standards.
- Tourism encourages small businesses and better infrastructure (roads, bridges) that locals also use. Geothermal power means cheaper electricity bills and more disposable income.
Positive environmental:
- Ash and lava break down and enrich soil, supporting forests, farms and wildlife habitats. New hills, lakes and viewpoints; rich biodiversity.
Negative economic:
- Farmers lost over EUR 3 million after Kanlaon's 2024 and 2025 eruptions. 300 hectares of farmland and 23,000 hectares of sugar cane damaged. Farmers could not work fields for weeks. Businesses hit by flight cancellations, water shortages and lower investor confidence. Repairs and relief strained government budgets.
- The 2020 Taal eruption caused about EUR 56 million damage to farming, fishing and aquaculture. Widespread rural job losses.
Negative social:
- Over 87,000 people evacuated during Kanlaon's eruptions. The 2020 Taal eruption affected over 736,000 people, with more than 135,000 displaced.
- Families in temporary shelters for long periods; schools and businesses closed; healthcare disrupted. Ash and sulphur dioxide caused health problems, especially for children and the elderly. Stress and uncertainty.
Negative environmental:
- Kanlaon's ash plumes reached up to 4,500 m, spreading thick layers over towns and countryside. Ash smothered crops, polluted rivers and harmed forests and aquatic life.
- Lahars (mudflows) and landslides destroyed fields and habitats.
- Mayon hazard map (Fig 6.37) shows lava flow and lahar flow zones around Mayon, with towns such as Legazpi City nearby.

EXAM SKILLS (SEC SAMPLE ANSWERS)
- Global North impacts question (economy/environment/society) answered with Iceland: economy - cheap geothermal energy cuts fuel imports, helps aluminium smelting and greenhouses; environment - geothermal energy cuts carbon footprint by 37%; society - evacuations such as Heimaey 1973 (800 people) break communities and cause stress.
- Irish landscape question: Antrim Plateau/Giant's Causeway (extrusive, divergent, 65 million years ago) and Leinster Batholith (intrusive, convergent, 400 million years ago), with labelled before/after diagrams.

rows.prompt: What is a dormant volcano?
options: One that is erupting at the moment
One that is not erupting now but could erupt again
One whose magma supply has been cut off
One that formed under the sea
rows.explanation: A dormant volcano is 'sleeping': it still has a magma supply and could erupt in the future.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an extinct volcano in Northern Ireland?
rows.explanation: Slemish in Co. Antrim is given as an example of an extinct volcano.

rows.prompt: Mt Fuji in Japan is given as an example of which type of volcano?
rows.explanation: The chapter lists Mt Fuji, Mt Kilimanjaro and Mt Teide as dormant volcanoes.

rows.prompt: What is the name for molten rock once it reaches the Earth's surface?
rows.explanation: Below ground it is magma; once it reaches the surface it is called lava.

rows.prompt: Which part of a volcano is the main passageway for magma to reach the surface?
rows.explanation: The central vent connects the magma chamber to the surface.

rows.prompt: What is a pyroclastic flow?
options: A fast cloud of hot gas, ash and rock
A slow river of runny basic lava
A jet of hot water and steam
A mudflow triggered by heavy rain
rows.explanation: Pyroclastic flows are clouds of hot gas, ash and rock that rush down a volcano, destroying everything.

rows.prompt: Which gas released by volcanoes is named as causing acid rain and breathing problems in Iceland?
rows.explanation: Sulphur dioxide from the Reykjanes eruptions exceeded health limits; volcanic gases can cause acid rain.

rows.prompt: What is a volcanic bomb?
options: A large piece of rock thrown out with force
A layer of fine grey powder
rows.explanation: Volcanic bombs are large pieces of rock emitted with force from the volcano.

rows.prompt: Roughly what is the silica content of acidic lava?
rows.explanation: Acidic lava has high silica (about 70%); basic lava has about 50%.

rows.prompt: Why are eruptions of acidic lava usually explosive?
options: Gases are trapped in the thick lava, so pressure builds
The lava is runny and flows very fast
The lava is low in silica
Gases escape easily from the vent
rows.explanation: Acidic lava is thick and sticky, trapping gases so pressure builds up until a violent eruption.

rows.prompt: High viscosity lava is best described as:
rows.explanation: High viscosity means thick, sticky lava that flows slowly, like honey.

rows.prompt: At a convergent boundary, what lowers the melting point of the mantle so magma forms?
options: Cold sea water at the trench
Water released from the sinking plate
rows.explanation: Minerals in the subducting plate release water, which lowers the mantle's melting point so it partly melts.

rows.prompt: Why does the oceanic plate sink beneath the continental plate?
options: It is colder at the surface
rows.explanation: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the less dense continental plate.

rows.prompt: The Andes are an example of which feature?
rows.explanation: The Andes form where an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate - a continental volcanic arc.

rows.prompt: About what percentage of the world's active volcanoes are in the Pacific Ring of Fire?
rows.explanation: The Ring of Fire is home to about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.

rows.prompt: What type of lava is found at divergent boundaries like Iceland?
rows.explanation: Magma at divergent boundaries is basic - low in silica and runny.

rows.prompt: Mid-ocean ridges account for over what share of global volcanic activity?
rows.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges are the sites of over 70% of global volcanic activity.

rows.prompt: Which volcano is given as an example of one found in a rift valley?
rows.explanation: Mt Kilimanjaro formed where magma rose through fissures in the East African Rift Valley.

rows.prompt: What is another name for the hot region in the mantle that forms a hotspot?
rows.explanation: A hotspot is caused by a mantle plume, an unusually hot region in the mantle.

rows.prompt: In the Hawaiian chain, which island is the oldest?
rows.explanation: The islands get older away from the hotspot; Kauai is the oldest and Hawaii the youngest.

rows.prompt: Why does an island volcano in a hotspot chain become extinct?
options: The mantle plume moves away from it
Sea water cools its magma chamber
The plate carries it away from its magma source
rows.explanation: The plume is fixed; the moving plate carries the volcano off the hotspot, cutting its magma supply.

rows.prompt: Which volcano is an example of a shield volcano?
rows.explanation: Mauna Loa (and Kilauea) in Hawaii are shield volcanoes built from runny basic lava.

rows.prompt: Paricutin in Mexico is an example of which landform?
rows.explanation: Paricutin is a cinder cone, built from cinders piling up around the vent.

rows.prompt: How is a caldera formed?
options: Thick lava piles up around a vent
The volcano top collapses into an empty magma chamber
Water is heated underground until it erupts
rows.explanation: A huge eruption empties the magma chamber; without support the top collapses into a bowl.

rows.prompt: Strokkur in Iceland is an example of which feature?
rows.explanation: Strokkur, like Old Faithful, is a geyser - a jet of superheated water and steam.

rows.prompt: Roughly how long ago did the Antrim Plateau form?
rows.explanation: The Antrim Plateau formed about 65 million years ago as the Eurasian and American plates separated.

rows.prompt: Why did the Giant's Causeway form hexagonal columns?
options: The basalt contracted and fractured as it cooled
Waves cut the rock into shapes
rows.explanation: As the lava cooled it contracted and fractured into hexagonal columns.

rows.prompt: Which rocks were formed when heat from the Leinster Batholith baked the surrounding shale and sandstone?
rows.explanation: The heat caused metamorphism, changing shale and sandstone into schist, slate and quartzite.

rows.prompt: What share of Icelandic homes get electricity from geothermal power?
rows.explanation: Geothermal power supplies electricity to 90% of Icelandic homes.

rows.prompt: What process drives volcanic activity in the Philippines?
options: Subduction of the Eurasian Plate beneath the Philippine Plate
Plates pulling apart at a mid-ocean ridge
A mantle plume in the middle of a plate
rows.explanation: The Eurasian Plate subducts beneath the Philippine Plate, on the Ring of Fire.

rows.prompt: How many people were displaced by the 2020 Taal eruption?
rows.explanation: Taal affected over 736,000 people and displaced more than 135,000.

rows.prompt: In which year was tourism lowest as a share of Iceland's GDP on the graph?
rows.explanation: Tourism fell to 2.8% of GDP in 2020, its lowest point on the graph.

rows.prompt: Give three differences between basic lava and acidic lava.
rows.model_answer: Basic lava has low silica (about 50%) and low viscosity, so it is runny, flows far and lets gases escape, giving gentle eruptions and shield volcanoes. Acidic lava has high silica (about 70%) and high viscosity, so it is thick and sticky, traps gas and gives violent eruptions that build steep stratovolcanoes.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words how magma forms at a subduction zone.
rows.model_answer: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the other plate into the mantle. Heat and pressure make minerals in it release water, which lowers the melting point of the mantle so it partly melts into magma. This magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it rises through the crust and erupts.

rows.prompt: Explain how a chain of volcanic islands such as Hawaii forms over a hotspot.
rows.model_answer: A fixed mantle plume makes superheated magma that breaks through the moving Pacific Plate to form a volcano. The plate carries the volcano away like a conveyor belt, so it loses its magma supply and becomes extinct while a new volcano forms over the hotspot. This leaves a line of islands, youngest (Hawaii, with Kilauea and Mauna Loa) over the hotspot and oldest (Kauai) furthest away.

rows.prompt: Draw and label a simple volcano (describe it in words), naming five parts.
rows.model_answer: A cone-shaped hill made of old layers of ash and lava sits on the Earth's crust. Underneath is the magma chamber, joined to the surface by the central vent, with a side vent branching off. At the top is the crater, from which lava flows and a cloud of steam, gas and ash rises.

rows.prompt: Describe how a geyser forms. Name one example.
rows.model_answer: Water seeps into underground chambers and is heated by hot rocks or magma. Trapped in narrow passages it becomes superheated and pressure builds until a jet of hot water and steam bursts out of the ground. The chamber then refills and the cycle repeats, e.g. Old Faithful in Yellowstone or Strokkur in Iceland.

rows.prompt: Explain how the Leinster Batholith came to be exposed at the surface.
rows.model_answer: It formed over 400 million years ago when the Eurasian and North American plates collided and magma cooled slowly underground into granite. Its heat baked the surrounding rock into metamorphic rock. Over millions of years uplift, weathering and erosion stripped away the overlying metamorphic cap, exposing the granite as dome-shaped mountains like Kippure.

rows.prompt: What is a lahar and what can trigger one?
rows.model_answer: A lahar is a fast-moving volcanic mudflow made of water, ash and rocks that travels down a volcano like wet concrete. It can be triggered by an eruption or by heavy rain. Lahars from Kanlaon destroyed fields and wildlife habitats.

rows.prompt: Why do Global South countries usually suffer worse impacts from eruptions than Global North countries?
rows.model_answer: Global North countries have strong infrastructure and effective disaster responses, so they face fewer casualties and less disruption. Global South countries often have poorer infrastructure, limited resources and weaker emergency planning, so they suffer higher death tolls, more people displaced and longer recovery times.

rows.prompt: Examine the formation of one volcanic landform. You may use a labelled diagram (describe it in words). (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Landform: the shield volcano, e.g. Mauna Loa in Hawaii. Shield volcanoes form at divergent boundaries and hotspots where magma is basic. Hawaii lies over a hotspot, a fixed mantle plume that makes superheated magma, which rises through the Pacific Plate. Basic lava is low in silica (about 50%) and has low viscosity, so it is runny. Gases escape easily, so eruptions are gentle, not explosive. The lava erupts from a central vent or from fissures and flows quickly over long distances. It spreads out in thin, wide layers before cooling. Over time repeated eruptions add more layers of solidified lava, building a broad, gently sloping mountain. Mauna Loa is about 180 km wide and over 4,100 m high. Diagram: a wide, low cone with gently sloping sides made of layers of solidified lava, a crater at the top, a vent leading down to a magma chamber below the crust.
rows.marking_scheme: Named landform 2m. Diagram 4m (2 marks for a clear drawing, 2 marks for at least 4 correct labels, e.g. vent, magma chamber, lava layers, gentle slope). Explanation: 7 SRPs x 2m = 14m (e.g. basic lava, low silica, low viscosity, gases escape/gentle eruptions, flows far, thin wide layers, repeated eruptions build layers, broad gentle slope, hotspot/divergent setting, named example detail). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain how volcanic activity occurs at convergent plate boundaries. Refer to example(s) in your answer. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Volcanic activity at convergent boundaries is caused by subduction. When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the less dense continental plate. In the Philippines, the Eurasian Plate is subducted beneath the Philippine Plate. As the plate sinks into the mantle, heat and pressure cause minerals in it to break down and release water. The water lowers the melting point of the mantle so it partly melts, forming magma. This magma is less dense than the surrounding rock and rises through the crust. The magma is acidic, with high silica (about 70%) and lots of gas. Because the lava is thick and sticky, gases are trapped and pressure builds, so eruptions are violent and explosive. Layers of acidic lava and ash build up near the vent, forming tall, steep-sided stratovolcanoes such as Kanlaon in the Philippines, which is over 2,500 m high. These volcanoes form chains parallel to the subduction zone called volcanic arcs. Continental volcanic arcs, like the Andes, form where an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate. Volcanic island arcs, like Japan and the Philippines, form where two oceanic plates meet. Stress also builds as the plates collide, causing frequent, powerful earthquakes. The Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific, contains about 75% of the world's active volcanoes because of subduction.
rows.marking_scheme: Name process (subduction) 2m. Named example(s) 2m (e.g. Philippines/Kanlaon, Andes, Japan, Ring of Fire). Explanation: 13 SRPs x 2m = 26m. Credit points such as: denser oceanic plate sinks; release of water; lowered melting point; partial melting forms magma; magma rises as less dense; acidic/high silica; trapped gas, explosive; stratovolcano formed; volcanic arcs (continental/island); earthquakes; Ring of Fire 75%; relevant statistics. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: With reference to a Global North location that you have studied, explain one impact of volcanic activity on each of the following: economy; environment; society. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Location: Iceland, on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Economy: heat from volcanic activity is used to make cheap, clean geothermal energy, supplying electricity to 90% of homes. This reduces the need for imported fossil fuels, lowering energy costs and protecting the economy from rising oil prices. Cheap energy gives industries such as aluminium smelting a competitive edge, and geothermal greenhouses allow year-round crops, reducing expensive food imports. Environment: geothermal energy is renewable, so Iceland burns less oil and gas. This has cut carbon dioxide emissions by up to 37%, helping to reduce climate change and improving air quality. However, recent Reykjanes eruptions (2023-2025) released sulphur dioxide above health limits in Reykjavik, and ash and lava can bury farmland and habitats. Society: eruptions force people to evacuate, sometimes for good. In 1973 the Heimaey eruption made 800 residents leave and never return, and in Grindavik in 2023-2024 hundreds were displaced. This breaks up communities, closes schools and healthcare, and causes fear and anxiety for families.
rows.marking_scheme: Named Global North location 2m (Iceland). Three impacts, each examined: Economy 9m, Environment 9m, Society 9m (impact identified 2m + 3 developed SRPs x 2m each, e.g. geothermal 90% homes, lower fuel imports, aluminium smelting, greenhouses; 37% CO2 cut, cleaner air; Heimaey 800 people, Grindavik displacement, stress, services closed). Discretion 1m for overall coherence. Total 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Examine the impacts of volcanic activity on the Irish landscape. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Two Irish landscapes show the impact of volcanic activity. First, the Antrim Plateau in Northern Ireland formed about 65 million years ago when the Eurasian and North American plates separated at a divergent boundary. This caused fissure eruptions: highly fluid, low-silica basic lava welled up through long cracks in the crust. As it was low in gas, eruptions were gentle and the lava spread over long distances. This went on and off for about 2 million years, building layers of basalt up to 1 km thick and forming a wide, flat lava plateau. As the basalt cooled it contracted and cracked into over 40,000 hexagonal columns, forming the Giant's Causeway, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Beneath the basalt lie older chalk and limestone laid down by shallow seas. Second, the Leinster Batholith formed over 400 million years ago when the Eurasian and North American plates collided. A huge mass of magma rose into the crust but did not reach the surface; it cooled slowly into coarse-grained granite. Its heat baked the surrounding shale and sandstone into metamorphic schist, slate and quartzite. Uplift and erosion removed the overlying rock, exposing the granite. The batholith stretches over 120 km and forms the core of the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains, with rounded granite mountains like Kippure and resistant metamorphic peaks like Lugnaquilla.
rows.marking_scheme: Two named Irish examples 2m + 2m (e.g. Antrim Plateau/Giant's Causeway; Leinster Batholith). Labelled diagram (if asked) or credit within SRPs. Examination: 13 SRPs x 2m = 26m, e.g. divergent boundary 65 million years; fissure eruptions; basic low-silica lava; gentle eruptions; basalt layers up to 1 km; contraction into hexagonal columns; UNESCO site; convergent collision 400 million years; magma cooling slowly into granite; metamorphism to schist/slate/quartzite; uplift and erosion exposing granite; 120 km core of Dublin-Wicklow Mountains; Kippure and Lugnaquilla. Total 30 marks.
